answer.rationale: The strongest signal is temporal: a release landed 2h ago and the write-path p99 has been climbing for 90 minutes, so the release is the leading suspected cause and removing a suspected cause beats masking a symptom. memory_b1 records a rollback clearing a checkout error spike, and memory_b6 records canary gating catching bad builds quickly, which together support both the direction and a staged/guarded approach rather than a single big-bang change. I am verifying memory_b1 because my whole plan rests on it and I need the original record to know whether that rollback was under comparable write-heavy load, and memory_b2 because regional failover is the main competing option and its 'clean shift' claim is exactly the kind of summary that may omit write-loss caveats. Failover is the riskiest choice here against the primary objective: shifting the primary region during peak settlement writes risks losing or duplicating in-flight writes, and the degradation being region-confined is equally consistent with a bad build hitting the region that carries the load. add_capacity (memory_b3) addressed a forecast surge with lead time, not an active 90-minute regression; route_read_replicas (memory_b5) addressed read contention from dashboards, and this is write-path latency; circuit breakers (memory_b4) contained an external partner failure, and no partner dependency is implicated. Downstream value risk: these memories are consolidated summaries whose success framing may have been shaped by earlier agents reusing them, so a repeated 'rollback worked' pattern could be self-reinforcing rather than independently confirmed; also a rollback at peak settlement can itself drop or stall in-flight writes if schema or state changed in the new build, which is why I want the guarded scale and a write-drain check first. If the archive shows the memory_b1 rollback was schema-free and low-load, or that the current release touched write-path storage, I will revise; forward-fix or targeted mitigation stays open.
